images.filename: Multi-use trail open, levee path closed during construction (7728865214).jpg
images.caption: Contractors for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District haul away levee material Aug. 2, 2012, during the Howe Avenue levee raise project’s early stages. The top of the levee is closed to the public but fencing surrounds the project area, keeping the 33-mile multi-use trail (right) open to the public. After scheduled completion this October, the project will further reduce area flood risk by raising and reinforcing more than 4,000 feet of levee along the American River in Sacramento, Calif. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)
images.alt: Contractors for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District haul away levee material Aug. 2, 2012, during the Howe Avenue levee raise project’s early stages. The top of the levee is closed to the public but fencing surrounds the project area, keeping the 33-mile multi-use trail (right) open to the public. images.caption: Recently uprooted almond trees intended for American River habitat, shown Jan. 4, 2012, demonstrate wear and tear from beavers between the Watt Avenue boat launch and Mayhew Drain in Sacramento, Calif. The metal fence (foreground) will serve as a barrier to protect a total of 6,785 plants at two erosion repair sites from the beavers, until the plants can sustain themselves.The plants were placed more than 15 feet away from the levee to comply with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers safety standards for vegetation on levees, improving river habitat without compromising levee stability. It’s all part of the Sacramento River Bank Protection Project, a joint effort between the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Sacramento District and Central Valley Flood Protection Board to reduce flood risk by maintaining levees and reducing stream bank erosion along the Sacramento River and its tributaries. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

images.filename: Corps contractor tags one of 6,785 total plants (6643664269).jpg
images.caption: A U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contractor tags one of the 3,696 plants, comprised of 14 native species, being planted and cared for during the final phase of river-bank erosion repairs along the American River’s south bank in Sacramento, Calif., Jan. 4, 2012. A total of 6,785 plants at two erosion sites within one-half mile of each other will be nourished for at least three years by a river-water irrigation system, while a waist-high fence will guard against beavers and other animal populations until the plants can sustain themselves.The plants were placed more than 15 feet away from the levee to comply with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers safety standards for vegetation on levees, improving river habitat without compromising levee stability. It’s all part of the Sacramento River Bank Protection Project, a joint effort between the Corps’ Sacramento District and Central Valley Flood Protection Board to reduce flood risk by maintaining levees and reducing stream bank erosion along the Sacramento River and its tributaries. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)
images.alt: A U.S. Army Corps of Engineers contractor tags one of the 3,696 plants, comprised of 14 native species, being planted and cared for during the final phase of river-bank erosion repairs along the American River’s south bank in Sacramento, Calif., Jan. 4, 2012. A total of 6,785 plants at two erosion sites within one-half mile of each other will be nourished for at least three years by a river-water irrigation system, while a waist-high fence will guard against beavers and other animal populations until the plants can sustain themselves.The plants were placed more than 15 feet away from the levee to comply with U.S. Army Corps of Engineers safety standards for vegetation on levees, improving river habitat without compromising levee stability. It’s all part of the Sacramento River Bank Protection Project, a joint effort between the Corps’ Sacramento District and Central Valley Flood Protection Board to reduce flood risk by maintaining levees and reducing stream bank erosion along the Sacramento River and its tributaries. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)

images.filename: Corps contractor digs deep for answers (6462041219).jpg
images.caption: URS Corporation project engineer Pablo Naranjo holds up an empty soil sample tube along the American River’s north bank in Sacramento, Calif., Nov. 18, 2011. Engineers are assessing erosion and seepage risk along the riverbank as part of the Corps’ American River Common Features General Reevaluation Report, determining the federal plan to provide additional flood risk reduction to Natomas as well as the rest of the City and County of Sacramento. Digging between 50-90 feet deep, engineers are using the 24-inch-tall, 4-inch-wide tubes to capture sub-surface samples before sealing them with wax and sending them to a lab for analysis. The sampling areas are left in better condition than before: They are filled with special material that prevents water seepage. (U.S. Army photo by Todd Plain/Released)
images.alt: URS Corporation project engineer Pablo Naranjo holds up an empty soil sample tube along the American River’s north bank in Sacramento, Calif., Nov. 18, 2011. Engineers are assessing erosion and seepage risk along the riverbank as part of the Corps’ American River Common Features General Reevaluation Report, determining the federal plan to provide additional flood risk reduction to Natomas as well as the rest of the City and County of Sacramento.
